Recovery identity is derived from user-controlled email or Host header
No throttling or lockout on OTP and security-question attempts
Token comparison is not constant-time or is exposed in URLs and logs

text: CWE-708: Incorrect Ownership Assignment. The product assigns an owner to a resource, but the owner lies outside the intended control sphere. The flawed assumption is that the creating process, the uploaded filename, or a client-supplied owner field determines ownership safely. In practice files inherit the wrong uid or gid, records are written with a tenant_id taken from the request, or a shared resource is reassigned to the last user who touched it. The result is that an attacker gains read, modify, or execute rights over data they should not control. SAST and WAFs miss it because the assignment is a normal write, not an injection.

metadata.title: CWE-708: Incorrect Ownership Assignment
root_causes: Ownership fields populated from client input instead of the authenticated principal
Incorrect uid, gid, or tenant assignment during file and record creation
Shared resources reassigned without resetting ownership on release

text: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling. The product allocates reusable resources on behalf of an actor without imposing intended limits on size or count. The flawed assumption is that clients behave rationally or that infrastructure autoscaling absorbs abuse. Unbounded pagination, array fields, file uploads, coupon generation, session creation, and password-reset requests all become economic denial-of-service or logic-abuse primitives. SAST and WAFs miss it because each request is individually valid and small; the attack is in aggregate volume or in a single oversized structured payload.

metadata.title: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
root_causes: No per-principal quota on resource creation or request rate
Unbounded array, page size, or upload size accepted from clients
Resource limits enforced only at the UI or client layer

text: CWE-826: Premature Release of Resource During Expected Lifetime. The product releases a resource while it is still intended to be used by itself or another actor. The flawed assumption is that a release call is safe once the immediate operation completes, ignoring other references, in-flight transactions, or pooled consumers. Sessions invalidated before dependent operations finish, database connections returned to the pool mid-transaction, locks released before commit, and files deleted while a handler still reads them all produce use-after-release behavior. SAST and WAFs miss it because release is a legitimate lifecycle call and the request sequence is normal.

metadata.title: CWE-826: Premature Release of Resource During Expected Lifetime
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-826: Premature Release of Resource During Expected Lifetime
root_causes: Release occurs before all references or in-flight operations complete
No reference counting or ownership tracking for pooled resources
Locks or sessions released outside the transaction boundary

text: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization. The product has a concurrent sequence requiring temporary exclusive access to a shared resource, but a timing window allows another sequence to modify it. The flawed assumption is that check-then-act is atomic, that a database read followed by a write is isolated, or that a single client sends requests sequentially. Coupon redemption, balance withdrawal, inventory reservation, and one-time token use are classic targets. SAST misses it because each code path is locally correct; WAFs miss it because every request is valid. The defect is the absent atomic boundary.

metadata.title: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization
root_causes: Check-then-act sequences without atomic compare-and-set or row locking
Application-level uniqueness checks without database constraints
No idempotency key on state-changing operations

text: CWE-602: Client-Side Enforcement of Server-Side Security. The product includes a server that relies on the client to implement a protection mechanism intended to protect the server. The flawed assumption is that the shipped client is trustworthy and that users cannot alter JavaScript, hidden fields, or local storage. Price calculation, role checks, quantity limits, and file-type validation implemented only in the browser are advisory. SAST and WAFs miss it because the server receives a syntactically valid request that simply omits or changes a client-side constraint.

metadata.title: CWE-602: Client-Side Enforcement of Server-Side Security
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-602: Client-Side Enforcement of Server-Side Security
root_causes: Security decisions enforced only in JavaScript or mobile client code
Server trusts hidden fields, local storage, or client-computed totals
No server-side revalidation of price, role, quantity, or file type

text: CWE-807: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision. The product uses a protection mechanism that relies on the existence or values of an input that an untrusted actor can modify. The flawed assumption is that cookies, headers, hidden fields, or query parameters are integrity-protected because the client normally sends them unchanged. When authentication or authorization decisions read these values directly, an attacker sets admin=1, role=admin, or X-Forwarded-For and bypasses the control. SAST and WAFs miss it because the input is a normal request field and the application logic appears deliberate.

metadata.title: CWE-807: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-807: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision
root_causes: Security decisions derived from client-controlled cookies, headers, or parameters
No server-side session state or signed integrity token
Trusting proxy headers from untrusted network positions

text: CWE-472: External Control of Assumed-Immutable Web Parameter. The web application does not sufficiently verify inputs assumed to be immutable but actually externally controllable, such as hidden form fields, cookies, and URL parameters. The flawed assumption is that values not rendered as editable inputs cannot be changed. Attackers use an intercepting proxy to alter price, user_id, role, discount, or status fields before submission. SAST and WAFs miss it because the parameter is part of a legitimate request and the server performs no malicious-pattern matching.

metadata.title: CWE-472: External Control of Assumed-Immutable Web Parameter
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-472: External Control of Assumed-Immutable Web Parameter
root_causes: Hidden fields and cookies trusted as server-authored state
No server-side canonical value or integrity check for submitted parameters
Business decisions based on client-retained values

text: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes. The product receives input specifying multiple attributes to initialize or update an object but does not control which attributes can be modified. The flawed assumption is that clients send only the fields shown in the UI. Frameworks that bind request bodies directly to models expose role, is_admin, balance, verified, and tenant_id for modification. SAST and WAFs miss it because the request is well-formed JSON and the extra keys are not attack syntax.

metadata.title: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes
root_causes: Request bodies bound directly to domain models without an allowlist
Framework auto-binding includes privileged or internal fields
No distinction between create and update DTOs

text: CWE-697: Incorrect Comparison. The product compares two entities in a security-relevant context, but the comparison is incorrect. The flawed assumption is that equality, ordering, and type coercion behave consistently across languages and encodings. Loose equality, case-insensitive matching, substring checks, null handling, and non-constant-time secret comparison create bypasses: 0e123 == 0e456, true == 1, admin == Admin, or a prefix match accepted as a full token. SAST may flag some comparisons, but WAFs miss the attack because it uses valid values, and many defects are semantic rather than syntactic.

metadata.title: CWE-697: Incorrect Comparison
root_causes: Loose equality or implicit type coercion in security checks
Case-insensitive or substring comparison used for exact-match secrets
Non-constant-time comparison of tokens or passwords
Missing null and type validation before comparison

text: CWE-384: Session Fixation. The application authenticates a user without invalidating the pre-authentication session identifier, so an attacker who can plant a known identifier can ride the victim's authenticated session. The flawed assumption is that a session ID is only meaningful after login and that clients cannot choose it; in practice IDs are accepted from URL parameters, cookies set by sibling subdomains, and session-adoption endpoints. The root cause is the absence of session rotation at the authentication boundary, often combined with predictable identifiers or URL-based session tracking. SAST and WAFs miss it because every request is a valid session operation and no malicious payload is required.

metadata.title: CWE-384: Session Fixation
root_causes: Session identifier is not rotated or invalidated at authentication
Session IDs accepted from URL parameters, cookies, or pre-auth requests
Predictable or reusable session identifiers enable fixation
No binding between the authenticated session and the post-login identifier

text: CWE-620: Unverified Password Change. The product allows a user to set a new password without proving knowledge of the current password or completing a fresh authentication step. The flawed assumption is that possession of a valid session is equivalent to knowing the credential, so a stolen session, CSRF, or a shared device is enough to take over the account. The root cause is a missing re-authentication check on the password-change path. SAST and WAFs miss it because the request is an ordinary authenticated form submission with no attack syntax.

metadata.title: CWE-620: Unverified Password Change
root_causes: Password change does not require the current password or step-up authentication
Session possession treated as proof of credential knowledge
No CSRF protection or session-freshness check on the change endpoint
Other sessions remain valid after a password change

text: CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption. The product does not properly control the allocation and maintenance of a limited resource, so an attacker can make a small request consume a disproportionate amount of CPU, memory, connections, or storage. The flawed assumption is that request volume or input size is bounded by the client, or that exhaustion only causes a graceful slowdown. The root cause is missing cost bounds, quotas, and lifetime management around expensive operations. SAST and WAFs miss it because each request is valid and the attack is in amplification, recursion, or resource lifetime rather than payload syntax.

metadata.title: CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
root_causes: Expensive operations lack cost bounds, depth limits, or timeouts
No per-principal quotas or rate limits on resource-consuming endpoints
Resource leaks or unbounded queues and connection pools
Fail-open behavior under resource exhaustion

text: CWE-667: Improper Locking. The product does not properly acquire or release a lock on a resource, producing unexpected state changes, deadlock, or data corruption. The flawed assumption is that locking is a local concern and that every path releases exactly once; double unlock, unlock without lock, lock-order inversion, missing locks, and user-controlled lock names all violate that assumption. The root cause is an inconsistent locking discipline across code paths. SAST and WAFs miss it because the defect is in concurrency control, not in request syntax.

metadata.title: CWE-667: Improper Locking
root_causes: Locks acquired and released on inconsistent code paths
Lock ordering inversion across concurrent operations
User-controlled or predictable lock names allow pre-acquisition
Missing timeouts and deadlock detection

text: CWE-1023: Incomplete Comparison with Missing Factors. The product compares two entities that must be evaluated across multiple factors, but the comparison omits one or more required dimensions. The flawed assumption is that one property, such as a scheme, path prefix, username, or identifier, is sufficient to establish equivalence or authorization. Examples include allowlists that block http and https but not ftp, path checks that compare a prefix without a boundary, and tenant checks that compare object IDs but not tenant IDs. SAST and WAFs miss it because the comparison is syntactically valid and the missing factor is semantic.

metadata.title: CWE-1023: Incomplete Comparison with Missing Factors
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-1023: Incomplete Comparison with Missing Factors
root_causes: Comparison omits a required factor such as scheme, tenant, path boundary, or type
Prefix, substring, or partial equality used for an exact-match decision
No canonicalization before comparison
Threat model does not enumerate all relevant comparison dimensions

text: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory (Path Traversal). The product builds a filesystem path from external input and intends it to stay beneath a restricted parent directory, but it fails to neutralize elements that escape that root: ../ sequences, absolute paths, drive letters, alternate separators, encoded variants, and null bytes. The flawed assumption is that a denylist for ../ is sufficient or that user-supplied names are only used as leaf filenames. Canonicalization happens after validation or not at all, so the check and the filesystem resolve the same string differently. SAST often misses it because the concatenation looks like ordinary file handling; WAFs miss encoded and double-encoded forms.

metadata.title: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory
root_causes: Path built by string concatenation from user input without canonicalization
Validation performed before decoding or before resolution, not after
Denylist for ../ only, omitting backslash, absolute paths, drive letters, and null bytes
Restricted root enforced only on the client or only for one endpoint

text: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command (OS Command Injection). The product assembles all or part of an operating-system command from externally influenced input without neutralizing metacharacters that alter the command before execution. The flawed assumption is that user input is a benign argument, so quoting is skipped or applied with an incomplete escape set. Semicolons, pipes, backticks, command substitution, newlines, and argument-injection switches turn a diagnostic feature into remote code execution under the service account. SAST frequently misses it because the call is a normal API invocation; WAFs miss encoded and shell-specific variants.

metadata.title: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command
root_causes: Shell invoked with a single concatenated string instead of an argument array
User input passed through system, popen, shell_exec, or backticks
Escape set incomplete for the target shell and platform
Argument injection accepted because input is not constrained to a strict allowlist

text: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command (SQL Injection). The product builds all or part of a SQL statement from externally influenced input without neutralizing syntax that changes the statement's meaning. The flawed assumption is that input is data, so string concatenation, dynamic ORDER BY or table names, and ORM raw fragments are treated as safe. In practice quotes, boolean operators, comment markers, unions, and stacked statements let an attacker read other rows, bypass authentication, modify data, or execute database functions. SAST misses dynamic identifiers and ORM escape hatches; WAFs miss encoded and comment-obfuscated payloads.

metadata.title: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command
root_causes: SQL built by string concatenation or interpolation with user input
Dynamic identifiers such as sort columns and table names not allowlisted
ORM raw-query escape hatches used with untrusted values
Database account has broader privileges than the feature requires

text: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (Cross-Site Scripting). The product places user-controllable input into a web page without neutralizing it for the output context, so a browser executes attacker-supplied script in the site's origin. The flawed assumption is that HTML-escaping everywhere is sufficient, ignoring that attribute, URL, JavaScript, and CSS contexts each need different encoding, and that DOM sinks such as innerHTML execute without any server involvement. Stored, reflected, and DOM-based variants all violate the same-origin boundary and can steal sessions, act as the victim, or rewrite the page. SAST misses DOM sinks and framework escape hatches; WAFs miss context-specific and encoded payloads.

metadata.title: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
root_causes: Output encoding missing or applied for the wrong context
User input written into DOM sinks such as innerHTML, document.write, or eval
Stored content rendered without sanitization in admin or support views
CSP absent or permissive, and session cookies not HttpOnly

text: CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data. The product reconstructs objects from data supplied by an untrusted source without ensuring the result is valid or safe. The flawed assumption is that serialized data is inert until the application inspects it; in reality many formats instantiate classes, invoke magic methods, and follow gadget chains during deserialization itself. Java ObjectInputStream, Python pickle, PHP unserialize, .NET BinaryFormatter, and unsafe YAML loaders can all execute code or trigger side effects before any validation runs. SAST misses gadget chains assembled across libraries; WAFs miss binary and encoded payloads.

metadata.title: CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data
root_causes: Native deserialization of data from cookies, requests, files, or queues
Gadget classes reachable on the classpath or autoloader
No integrity check or signature on serialized blobs
Unsafe YAML, XML, or format loaders used for configuration

text: CWE-352: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). The application accepts a state-changing request without verifying that the request was intentionally issued by the authenticated user. The flawed assumption is that a valid session cookie proves intent, but browsers attach cookies automatically to any request a page initiates, including cross-origin form posts, image tags, and fetch calls. The root cause is the absence of an unpredictable, per-request or per-session anti-CSRF token bound to the user, often combined with SameSite=None cookies and GET-based state changes. SAST rarely flags it because each handler looks like a normal authenticated action; WAFs miss it because the request is well-formed and carries no payload signature.

metadata.title: CWE-352: Cross-Site Request Forgery
root_causes: No anti-CSRF token on state-changing requests
Session cookie sent with SameSite=None or no SameSite attribute
State changes reachable via GET or simple form posts
Origin and Referer headers not validated as defense in depth

text: CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type. The product accepts an uploaded file and later processes or serves it in a context where its type is dangerous: a .php or .jsp file inside the web root, an .shtml file with server-side includes, an SVG that executes script, or an archive that is unpacked. The flawed assumption is that the browser-supplied Content-Type or the filename extension reflects the real type, or that uploads are harmless because they are "only images". The root cause is missing type enforcement based on content, no renaming, and storage inside an executable path. SAST misses it because the upload handler is ordinary I/O; WAFs miss polyglot and double-extension payloads.

metadata.title: CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
root_causes: File type validated only by extension or client-supplied Content-Type
User-supplied filename used directly, enabling double extensions and traversal
Uploads stored inside the web root or an executable directory
No content inspection, re-encoding, or size and count limits

text: CWE-611: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference (XXE). The product parses an XML document that may declare external entities whose URIs resolve outside the intended sphere of control, so the parser reads local files, performs network requests, or expands recursive entities. The flawed assumption is that XML input is data-only and that the parser's defaults are safe; in many runtimes external entity resolution is enabled by default for compatibility. The root cause is a parser configuration that permits DTDs and external entities, often hidden inside a library or an SVG, SOAP, or Office document upload. SAST misses it because the parse call is ordinary; WAFs miss encoded and parameter-entity variants.

metadata.title: CWE-611: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-611: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference
root_causes: XML parser left with DTD and external entity resolution enabled
User-controlled XML accepted without schema restriction
SOAP, SVG, or document parsers using unsafe defaults
No egress filtering to block parser-initiated network access

text: CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). The server accepts a URL or host from an upstream component and fetches it without ensuring the destination is the intended one. The flawed assumption is that users supply public URLs, so internal addresses, link-local metadata endpoints, and redirects are unconsidered. The root cause is destination validation based on string matching rather than resolved-address checks, combined with unrestricted egress. Attackers reach cloud metadata services, internal admin panels, and localhost-only services, or use the server as a proxy for scanning and data exfiltration. SAST misses it because the fetch is a normal HTTP client call; WAFs miss DNS rebinding and redirect chains.

metadata.title: CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery
root_causes: Destination validated by string or prefix match instead of resolved IP classification
Redirects followed without re-validating each hop
No egress policy blocking private, link-local, and metadata ranges
Full response bodies returned to the user

text: CWE-1333: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity (ReDoS). The product applies a regular expression whose worst-case complexity is exponential or polynomial in the input length, so a small crafted string drives catastrophic backtracking and consumes CPU for seconds or minutes. The flawed assumption is that regex matching is cheap and linear, and that input length limits alone prevent abuse. The root cause is nested or overlapping quantifiers over untrusted input, often in validators for email, URLs, user agents, or markup. SAST may flag some patterns but misses library regexes and dynamically composed ones; WAFs see a syntactically valid value.

metadata.title: CWE-1333: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity
root_causes: Nested or overlapping quantifiers such as (a+)+ or (.*a){n}
Unbounded input length passed to a backtracking regex engine
Regex applied per field, per line, or per element without limits
No backtracking or execution-time budget configured

text: WSTG-ATHN-01 examines whether authentication credentials cross the network without confidentiality protection. The application may serve the login page over HTTP, accept a form action pointing to an HTTP endpoint, or load authentication JavaScript from an insecure origin so that a mixed-content downgrade exposes the submission. Even when the landing page uses HTTPS, a redirect to HTTP, an insecure cookie scope, or a third-party identity endpoint without TLS can expose the password and session token. The weakness is architectural rather than syntactic: the credential is valid and the request is well-formed, but anyone on the path can read or alter it.

metadata.title: Cleartext Credential Transport and Mixed-Content Authentication
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-319: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information
root_causes: Login form or API served over HTTP
TLS terminated but mixed content downgrades the page
Credentials posted to a third-party or alternate host without TLS
Insecure redirect from HTTPS to HTTP during authentication

text: WSTG-ATHN-02 tests whether any account still accepts a vendor-supplied or well-known default credential. Defaults survive because installers create administrative accounts, demo users, and integration service accounts without forcing a change, and because documentation publishes the values. The risk is concentrated in management consoles, databases, message brokers, and appliances that are reachable from the application network. The flaw is not a broken authentication algorithm but an operational failure to remove a shared secret that attackers can look up. Automated scanners and botnets routinely try these pairs first.

metadata.title: Default and Vendor-Supplied Credential Exposure
root_causes: Administrative interfaces shipped with vendor defaults
Installers that do not force credential change
Demo accounts left enabled in production
Shared service accounts with published passwords

text: WSTG-ATHN-03 evaluates whether repeated authentication failures are bounded. A weak mechanism permits unlimited guesses, resets after a trivial event, or applies only per IP so that distributed or header-rotating attempts bypass it. Conversely, an over-aggressive lockout keyed solely on the username lets an attacker deny service to any known account. The weakness is a control-design problem: the password may be strong, but the system allows an attacker to test enough candidates, or to lock out legitimate users, without cost.

metadata.title: Weak Account Lockout and Brute-Force Resistance
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
root_causes: No per-account or per-source attempt limit
Lockout keyed only on username, enabling denial of service
Counter reset by a new session or header change
Unlimited parallel attempts across distributed endpoints

text: WSTG-ATHN-04 checks whether authentication can be bypassed rather than broken. Common causes include a protected page reachable directly, a filter that matches only certain path prefixes, an alternate HTTP method or host that skips the filter, a debug parameter that disables checks, or authentication enforced only in JavaScript. The application may also trust a client-supplied flag such as authenticated=true or a header injected by an upstream proxy. The defect is inconsistent enforcement: the login works, but some routes or request shapes never consult it.

metadata.title: Authentication Schema Bypass and Alternate Path Weakness
root_causes: Protected resources reachable without the auth filter
Client-side-only authentication gates
Parameter or header that toggles authenticated state
Inconsistent enforcement across routes, methods, or hosts

text: WSTG-ATHN-05 examines persistent login features that store or derive credentials in a way an attacker can recover or forge. A remember-me cookie may contain the password in clear text or weak encoding, a token built from a hash of the username, or a long-lived value that never rotates and cannot be revoked. Because the cookie survives logout and password change, theft of the device or cookie yields durable access. The weakness is the persistence design, not the initial login.

metadata.title: Insecure Remember-Password and Persistent Login Tokens
root_causes: Password stored in a persistent cookie
Remember-me token derived predictably from the username
Long-lived token without rotation or revocation
Token not bound to device or session

text: WSTG-ATHN-06 checks whether authenticated or sensitive responses can be recovered from browser history, the back-forward cache, disk cache, or shared intermediary caches. When pages carrying personal data, tokens, or one-time codes omit no-store directives, the content persists after logout and can be recovered by the next user of the device or by a proxy. Autocomplete and password manager behavior can also retain values the application intended to be transient. The defect is a missing cache policy on responses that must not be stored.

metadata.title: Browser and Intermediary Cache Exposure of Authenticated Content
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-525: Use of Web Browser Cache Containing Sensitive Information
root_causes: Authenticated responses lack Cache-Control: no-store
Sensitive pages cached by shared proxies
Back button reveals content after logout
History or autocomplete retains credentials

text: WSTG-ATHN-07 assesses whether the application enforces a password policy strong enough to resist guessing and credential stuffing. Weak policies allow short passwords, common passwords, or trivial patterns, and often rely on composition rules that produce predictable variants such as Password1!. The policy may exist only in client-side JavaScript and be bypassed by posting directly. Because reused and breached passwords dominate real attacks, the absence of a breached-password check is often more significant than complexity rules.

metadata.title: Weak Password Policy and Credential Quality Enforcement
root_causes: Short minimum length or no length requirement
No check against breached or common password lists
Composition rules without length or blocklist
Policy enforced only in the client

text: WSTG-ATHN-08 examines knowledge-based authentication used for recovery or step-up. Security questions often ask for facts available on social media, have a small answer space, or are checked with loose normalization that makes guessing easier. Because the recovery flow grants account control, a weak question is equivalent to a weak password that the attacker can research. The problem is the premise: static personal facts are not secrets, and users often provide the same answer across services.

metadata.title: Weak Security Question and Knowledge-Based Recovery
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-640: Weak Password Recovery Mechanism for Forgotten Password
root_causes: Questions with publicly discoverable answers
Answers normalized case-insensitively without rate limits
Small answer space brute-forceable
Recovery grants full account control

text: WSTG-ATHN-09 evaluates both the authenticated change flow and the unauthenticated reset flow. A change function that does not require the current password lets a stolen session take over the account, while a reset function with reusable, predictable, or leaked tokens lets an attacker set a new password remotely. Header-driven reset links enable poisoning, and sessions that survive a password change leave the attacker with persistent access. These are control-flow defects in a legitimate feature.

metadata.title: Weak Password Change and Reset Functionality
root_causes: Change does not require the current password
Reset token reusable, long-lived, or predictable
Reset link host derived from request headers
No session invalidation after change

text: WSTG-ATHN-10 looks for alternate channels that authenticate the same account with weaker controls than the primary web flow. A mobile API may skip MFA, a support desk may reset a password after weak verification, an IVR may accept a PIN, or a legacy endpoint may still accept security questions. Attackers pivot to the weakest channel, so the effective authentication strength of an account is the minimum across all channels. The defect is policy drift between interfaces that share one identity.

metadata.title: Weaker Authentication in Alternative Channels
root_causes: Mobile or API channel omits MFA
Support or IVR channel resets without strong proof
Legacy endpoint accepts weaker credentials
Channel-specific policy drift

text: WSTG-SESS-01 reviews the overall session management schema: how identifiers are generated, transported, stored, and expired. Weak schemes use short or predictable identifiers, embed user data without integrity protection, keep state entirely in unsigned client-side cookies, or never expire idle sessions. The consequence is that an attacker can guess, forge, or reuse a session to become the user. The weakness is systemic rather than a single bug, and it undermines every downstream authorization decision that trusts the session.

metadata.title: Session Management Schema Weaknesses
root_causes: Session identifier lacks sufficient entropy
Identifier predictable or derived from user data
Session state stored client-side without integrity
No lifecycle policy for creation, rotation, and expiry

text: WSTG-SESS-02 checks the attributes of session and sensitive cookies. A missing Secure flag allows the cookie to travel over HTTP; a missing HttpOnly flag exposes it to JavaScript and XSS; an absent or None SameSite value enables cross-site sending; and an overbroad Domain or Path scope leaks the cookie to sibling applications. These flags are defense in depth, but their absence turns a minor script-injection or network flaw into full session compromise. The defect is configuration, not application logic.

metadata.title: Insecure Session Cookie Attributes
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-614: Sensitive Cookie in HTTPS Session Without Secure Attribute
root_causes: Session cookie missing Secure or HttpOnly
SameSite absent or set to None without justification
Overly broad Domain or Path scope
Long expiry on a session cookie

text: WSTG-SESS-03 tests whether an attacker can plant a session identifier that becomes authenticated after the victim logs in. The application accepts an identifier from a URL, a hidden field, or a cookie set by a sibling subdomain, and does not issue a new identifier at authentication. The victim authenticates into the attacker-known session, and the attacker reuses it. The defect is the missing rotation at the authentication boundary, sometimes compounded by session adoption features and URL-based tracking.

metadata.title: Session Fixation Through Identifier Adoption
root_causes: Identifier not rotated at authentication
Identifier accepted from URL or request parameter
Session adoption endpoint trusts client-supplied ID
Sibling subdomain can set the cookie

text: WSTG-SESS-04 looks for session identifiers and sensitive variables exposed beyond the cookie boundary: in URLs, query strings, hidden fields, logs, referrer headers, analytics, and error output. URL-borne tokens leak through browser history, bookmarks, shared links, and the Referer header to third-party resources. Hidden fields may be replayed or tampered with if they are the sole carrier of session state. The defect is exposure of a secret to channels that were not designed to protect it.

metadata.title: Exposed Session Variables and Sensitive Token Leakage
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-598: Use of GET Request Method With Sensitive Query Strings
root_causes: Session token placed in a URL or query string
Token written to logs, referrer, or analytics
Token exposed in a hidden field without binding
Debug output or error page reveals session data

text: WSTG-SESS-05 verifies that session-bound state changes require proof of user intent. Because browsers attach cookies automatically, any cross-origin page can trigger a request in the victim's session. The application is vulnerable when it relies on the cookie alone, accepts state changes over GET, or uses SameSite=None to support cross-site embedding. The defect is the absence of an unpredictable, session-bound token and complementary origin checks, which turns a passive victim visit into an authenticated action.

metadata.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery in Session-Bound Operations
root_causes: No anti-CSRF token on state-changing requests
SameSite=None session cookie
GET endpoints mutate state
Origin and Referer not validated

text: WSTG-SESS-06 evaluates whether logout actually terminates the session. Many applications delete the client cookie while leaving the server-side session valid, so a captured identifier still works. Others keep remember-me tokens, API tokens, and federated sessions alive, or allow the Back button to render cached authenticated pages. The defect is an incomplete lifecycle transition: the user believes access ended, but the credential remains usable. This matters on shared devices and after token theft.

metadata.title: Incomplete Logout and Session Termination
root_causes: Logout clears the cookie but not server-side state
Other sessions and tokens remain valid
Back button restores authenticated content
Logout reachable only by GET without CSRF protection

text: WSTG-SESS-07 measures whether sessions expire after inactivity and after an absolute maximum lifetime. Applications that rely on client-side timers, never expire idle sessions, or extend the lifetime on every request leave a stolen identifier usable for days. Sensitive applications also need re-authentication for high-risk actions even within an active session. The defect is a missing or unenforced lifecycle bound, which increases the window for session theft and shared-device misuse.

metadata.title: Insufficient Session Timeout and Idle Expiration
root_causes: No idle timeout or an excessively long one
No absolute session lifetime
Timeout enforced only client-side
Activity extends the session indefinitely

text: WSTG-SESS-08 examines session puzzling, where an application reuses the same session variables across different features or stages, so state from one context influences another. A value set during registration or password reset may remain in the session and alter authorization after login, or a parameter accepted by one module may be trusted by another. The defect is missing namespace separation and lifecycle hygiene for session state, allowing an attacker to prime a variable and have it consumed elsewhere.

metadata.title: Session Puzzling and Variable Reuse Across Contexts
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-488: Exposure of Data Element to Wrong Session
root_causes: Session variables reused across different flows
State set before authentication persists after login
Shared session keys across modules
No namespace separation between contexts

text: WSTG-SESS-09 assesses whether a stolen session token can be replayed from another context. Hijacking vectors include XSS reading document.cookie, cleartext transmission, malware or shared-device access, and predictable or leaked identifiers. Applications that do not bind sessions to a device, rotate tokens, or detect concurrent use from distant locations allow a stolen token to be used indefinitely. The defect is the lack of contextual binding and detection around a bearer credential.

metadata.title: Session Hijacking via Token Theft and Replay
root_causes: Session token exposed to script or network
No binding to device or network context
Token accepted from any location
No anomaly detection on concurrent use

text: WSTG-CRYP-01 evaluates the TLS configuration of endpoints that carry credentials or sensitive data. Weak configurations permit TLS 1.0 or 1.1, export or NULL ciphers, RC4, 3DES, small RSA keys, or invalid certificates, and clients may disable validation entirely. The result is that an active attacker can downgrade or decrypt traffic, or impersonate the server. The flaw is configuration drift and legacy compatibility, not the protocol itself, and it is often invisible to application-level testing.

metadata.title: Weak Transport Layer Security Configuration
root_causes: Legacy TLS versions enabled
Weak cipher suites and small keys
Certificate validation disabled on the client
No HSTS or secure renegotiation

text: WSTG-CRYP-02 tests for padding oracle weaknesses in CBC-based encryption. When decryption distinguishes invalid padding from invalid content through an error, status code, or timing difference, an attacker can decrypt ciphertext or forge it byte by byte without the key. The root cause is unauthenticated encryption and observable failure modes; the fix is an AEAD mode or encrypt-then-MAC with uniform error handling. The flaw is subtle because the application appears to handle errors correctly.

metadata.title: Padding Oracle and Missing Integrity Checking
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-353: Missing Support for Integrity Check
root_causes: CBC mode without authenticated encryption
Distinct errors for padding versus content
Decryption oracle exposed through responses or timing
No MAC over ciphertext

text: WSTG-CRYP-03 checks whether sensitive information travels over channels without confidentiality protection. Beyond the login form, this includes personal data in API calls, tokens in URLs, email over plain SMTP, database connections without TLS, and telemetry or analytics payloads. The weakness is that the data is readable and modifiable by anyone on the path, and it often persists in logs and caches. The defect is a channel-selection and configuration failure rather than a broken cipher.

metadata.title: Sensitive Information Sent Over Unencrypted Channels
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-319: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information
root_causes: Sensitive data sent over HTTP or SMTP without TLS
Non-TLS service ports exposed
Cleartext in cookies or URL parameters
Third-party integrations without TLS

text: WSTG-CRYP-04 identifies cryptographic algorithms and modes that no longer provide the intended security. MD5 and SHA-1 are unsuitable for signatures and password storage, DES and RC4 are broken, ECB leaks structure, and fixed IVs or keys undermine otherwise strong primitives. Home-grown schemes frequently combine these errors. The defect is often invisible because the data looks encrypted; the weakness is in the construction, not the presence of a cryptographic call.

metadata.title: Weak or Broken Cryptographic Algorithms
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm
root_causes: MD5 or SHA-1 for security purposes
DES, RC4, or ECB mode
Hard-coded keys or IVs
Home-grown cryptography

text: WSTG-INPV-01 tests whether a request parameter is reflected into a response in an executable context. Reflected XSS is immediate and non-persistent: the payload travels in the URL or body and is written into HTML, an attribute, a script block, or a DOM sink without correct encoding. Attackers deliver a crafted link to a victim, and the script runs in the target origin. The root cause is output encoding for the wrong context or reliance on a denylist, which encoding tricks and alternate tags bypass.

metadata.title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting in Request Parameters
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
root_causes: Request parameter echoed without context-aware encoding
Error and search pages reflect raw input
Client-side sink writes location data to innerHTML
Incomplete denylist of script tags

text: WSTG-INPV-02 tests whether input stored by the application is later rendered to other users without neutralization. Stored XSS is more dangerous than reflected because it requires no crafted link: every viewer of the affected page executes the payload. Common carriers are profile names, comments, support tickets, filenames, and admin dashboards that render user content. The root cause is missing sanitization or an allowlist sanitizer that can be bypassed, combined with rendering contexts that differ from where the data was validated.

metadata.title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting in Persisted Content
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
root_causes: Persisted fields rendered without sanitization
Rich-text sanitizer missing or bypassable
Admin and support views render raw content
HTML injection allowed in names and comments

text: WSTG-INPV-03 tests whether access control depends on the HTTP method in a way an attacker can change. A filter may protect POST /admin but not GET, HEAD, PUT, or a method-override header, and some frameworks route every method to the same handler while the security constraint names only one. The result is that a protected action is reachable with a different verb or with X-HTTP-Method-Override. The defect is inconsistent method handling between the authorization layer and the application router.

metadata.title: HTTP Verb Tampering and Method-Based Access Gaps
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-650: Trusting HTTP Permission Methods on the Server Side
root_causes: Authorization filter scoped to specific methods
Framework routes all methods to the same handler
HEAD or OPTIONS bypasses the auth check
Method override headers honored without validation

text: WSTG-INPV-04 tests how the application handles repeated or ambiguous parameters. When a WAF, proxy, framework, and backend disagree about whether to use the first, last, or combined value, an attacker can smuggle a malicious value past inspection or change business logic. HPP affects authorization, price calculation, and filtering. The defect is inconsistent parsing across tiers, not a single injection flaw, and it is often invisible to scanners that send each parameter once.

metadata.title: HTTP Parameter Pollution and Duplicate Parameter Handling
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-235: Improper Handling of Extra Parameters
root_causes: Duplicate parameters resolved differently by tiers
Framework takes first value, backend takes last
Parameter names not canonicalized
WAF inspects a different occurrence than the application

text: WSTG-INPV-05 tests whether user input can alter SQL statement structure. The application may concatenate input into WHERE clauses, ORDER BY, LIMIT, or identifiers, or use ORM raw fragments that bypass parameter binding. Successful injection reads other rows, bypasses authentication, modifies data, or executes database functions. The defect is the mixing of code and data in query construction; input validation alone does not fix it when free-form text must be accepted.

metadata.title: SQL Injection in Query Construction
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command
root_causes: String-concatenated SQL with user input
Dynamic identifiers not allowlisted
ORM raw fragments with interpolation
Over-privileged database account

text: WSTG-INPV-06 tests whether input can alter an LDAP filter. Directory searches are built as filters such as (&(uid=<user>)(userPassword=<pass>)); if input is concatenated without escaping, characters like *, (, ), and | change the filter's logic. An attacker can bypass authentication, enumerate directory entries, or broaden a search to return every user. The defect is the same code-data mixing as SQL injection, applied to a different query language.

metadata.title: LDAP Injection in Directory Queries
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-90: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an LDAP Query
root_causes: LDAP filter built by string concatenation
User input not escaped for filter metacharacters
Authentication filter accepts wildcards
Directory account over-privileged

text: WSTG-INPV-07 tests whether user input can alter the structure or meaning of an XML document. When input is concatenated into XML without escaping, characters such as <, >, and & inject elements, attributes, or comments, changing what a downstream parser sees. This can escalate privileges, bypass signature checks, or combine with XXE. The defect is missing output encoding or schema validation at the point where XML is constructed.

metadata.title: XML Injection and Document Structure Manipulation
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-91: XML Injection (aka Blind XPath Injection)
root_causes: User input concatenated into XML documents
No schema validation on generated XML
Parser accepts duplicate or injected elements
External entities left enabled

text: WSTG-INPV-08 tests whether user input can introduce server-side include directives that the web server executes. SSI directives such as <!--#exec cmd=... --> and <!--#include file=... --> are processed before the response is sent, so injection can execute commands or read local files. Risk arises when SSI is enabled on upload directories, user content, or templates that reflect input. The defect is a dangerous server feature applied to untrusted content.

metadata.title: Server-Side Include Injection
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-97: Improper Neutralization of Server-Side Includes (SSI) Within a Web Page
root_causes: SSI processing enabled on user-writable content
Uploaded files served with SSI handler
Input reflected into an .shtml template
No output encoding for SSI directives

text: WSTG-INPV-09 tests whether input can alter an XPath expression used to query XML data. Expressions such as //user[username='INPUT' and password='INPUT'] are vulnerable when input is concatenated, because a quote and boolean clause change the predicate. Attackers bypass authentication or walk the XML tree to extract other nodes. The defect mirrors SQL injection but targets XML stored in files, configuration, or in-memory documents.

metadata.title: XPath Injection in XML Data Queries
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-643: Improper Neutralization of Data within XPath Expressions
root_causes: XPath expression built by concatenation
Quotes and brackets not escaped
Authentication query accepts boolean injection
Detailed errors reveal the expression

text: WSTG-INPV-10 tests whether input reaches an IMAP or SMTP command stream without neutralizing CRLF and protocol metacharacters. Applications that build mailbox queries or send mail from user-supplied addresses can be tricked into injecting additional commands, copying messages, changing headers, or relaying spam. The defect is the same code-data mixing as other injection classes, applied to line-oriented mail protocols where a newline terminates the command.

metadata.title: IMAP and SMTP Command Injection
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-93: Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences
root_causes: User input concatenated into mail protocol commands
CRLF not rejected in addresses or subjects
Mail client passes input to a command channel
No protocol-aware escaping

text: WSTG-INPV-11 tests whether user input is interpreted as code or controls which code file is loaded. Direct code injection occurs when eval, assert, or a template expression evaluates input. File inclusion occurs when an include or require path comes from a parameter, allowing local files or remote URLs to be executed. Both collapse the boundary between data and code, so a request becomes program execution. The defect is dynamic evaluation or dynamic include of untrusted values.

metadata.title: Code Injection Including Local and Remote File Inclusion
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')
root_causes: User input evaluated by a language interpreter
Dynamic include path derived from a parameter
Allow URL or file wrappers in include functions
Uploaded code reachable by the interpreter

text: WSTG-INPV-12 tests whether user input reaches an operating system command without neutralization. Features such as ping, DNS lookup, image conversion, and archive extraction often call external programs with a concatenated string. Metacharacters then execute additional commands under the service account. Filtering is frequently incomplete across shells and platforms, and argument injection can add dangerous switches even without a shell. The defect is the absence of a structured argument interface.

metadata.title: Operating System Command Injection
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command
root_causes: Shell invoked with a concatenated string
User input passed to system or popen
Incomplete metacharacter filtering
Argument injection into wrapped binaries

text: WSTG-INPV-13 tests whether user input is used as a format string rather than as an argument to it. Calling printf(user_input) instead of printf('%s', user_input) lets %s, %x, and %n read stack memory, crash the process, or write to arbitrary addresses in native code. Higher-level languages can also misinterpret format specifiers in logging and localization libraries. The defect is a misplaced argument: data occupies the position reserved for the format.

metadata.title: Format String Injection
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-134: Use of Externally-Controlled Format String
root_causes: User input used as the format argument
printf-family call with a dynamic string
Logging APIs that treat input as a format
No validation of conversion specifiers

text: WSTG-INPV-14 tests for incubated, or second-order, vulnerabilities: input that is harmless at the point of entry but dangerous when consumed later by another component, job, or view. A value may pass registration validation, be stored, and then be interpolated into a query, shell command, or HTML by a reporting service that trusts the database. The defect is inconsistent trust across time and components, which point-in-time scanners miss because the entry request shows no immediate effect.

metadata.title: Incubated and Second-Order Vulnerabilities
root_causes: Input validated at entry but trusted later
Stored data consumed by a different component
Sanitization applied only on first render
Batch or background jobs process unvalidated data

text: WSTG-INPV-15 tests whether crafted HTTP messages are parsed differently by intermediaries and origin servers. Response splitting injects CRLF into a header to create a second response, enabling cache poisoning and script injection. Request smuggling exploits disagreement over Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding so that part of one request is treated as the start of the next, poisoning queues and bypassing access controls. The defect is inconsistent HTTP parsing across the chain.

metadata.title: HTTP Splitting and Request Smuggling
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-444: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling')
root_causes: CRLF accepted in header values
Front-end and back-end disagree on Content-Length versus Transfer-Encoding
Conflicting duplicate headers
No normalization of obs-fold or whitespace

text: WSTG-INPV-16 examines how the application handles unusual incoming HTTP requests, including absolute-form targets, unexpected methods, proxy-style requests, and malformed paths. A server that accepts absolute URLs can act as a proxy or reach internal services; one that mishandles CONNECT or OPTIONS may expose capabilities outside the intended surface. The defect is an overly permissive request parser or unintended intermediary role, which turns the web tier into a confused deputy.

metadata.title: Unexpected HTTP Incoming Request Handling
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-441: Unintended Proxy or Intermediary ('Confused Deputy')
root_causes: Server accepts absolute-form request targets
Proxy behavior enabled unintentionally
Unvalidated Host and method handling
Internal services reachable through the web tier

text: WSTG-INPV-17 tests whether the application trusts the Host header or forwarding headers to build URLs, route requests, or make security decisions. Password-reset links generated from Host can be poisoned to deliver tokens to an attacker; virtual-host routing can reach unintended applications; cache keys may be influenced. The defect is treating a client-supplied header as authoritative server configuration.

metadata.title: Host Header Injection and Trusted Header Abuse
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-644: Improper Neutralization of HTTP Headers for Scripting Syntax
root_causes: Reset links built from the Host header
Virtual host routing trusts unvalidated Host
X-Forwarded-Host honored from untrusted clients
Absolute URLs derived from request headers

text: WSTG-INPV-18 tests whether user input is compiled as part of a server-side template rather than passed as data. When input such as {{7*7}} is rendered by Jinja2, Twig, Freemarker, or Velocity, the engine evaluates it, and a sufficiently expressive context allows reading files, executing commands, or accessing secrets. The defect is template source controlled by the user, often through preview, email, or report features. Escaping output does not help because the input is code, not data.

metadata.title: Server-Side Template Injection
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-1336: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine
root_causes: User input concatenated into a template
Template rendered with untrusted data as source
Framework exposes template evaluation to users
Sandbox misconfigured or escapable

text: WSTG-INPV-19 tests whether the server can be induced to fetch attacker-chosen destinations. Features such as URL previews, webhooks, imports, and image proxies accept a URL and retrieve it; without destination validation the server reaches localhost, private networks, and cloud metadata. String filters are bypassed with redirects, alternate IP encodings, and DNS rebinding. The defect is the absence of resolved-address validation and egress control around a server-initiated request.

metadata.title: Server-Side Request Forgery
root_causes: URL fetched without destination validation
String-based allowlist bypassable
Redirects followed without revalidation
No egress restrictions

text: The OAuth implicit flow returns an access token and identity claims directly to the browser, and this client accepts the resulting email as proof of identity. After the provider redirects back, the client posts the email to an authentication endpoint that creates a session without verifying the token signature, issuer, audience, or subject. An attacker completes the flow with their own social account and rewrites the email to a victim's address, receiving a session for that victim. The defect is trust in a client-controlled identity claim rather than a server-validated token bound to the authenticated subject.

metadata.title: OAuth Implicit Flow Identity Spoofing
root_causes: Client trusts the email claim delivered through the implicit flow
No server-side validation that the token was issued to the submitted identity
Implicit flow returns identity data directly to the browser
Session established from a client-supplied POST parameter

text: The account-linking feature attaches a social profile to the logged-in account through an OAuth flow that has no CSRF protection. Because the flow does not bind a state value to the victim's session, an attacker can complete the provider authorization with their own social account, pause before the final linking request, and deliver that request to the victim. The victim's active session completes the link, so the attacker's social identity now authenticates into the victim's account. The defect is a missing anti-CSRF binding on a security-sensitive identity mutation.

metadata.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery in OAuth Account Linking
root_causes: Profile-linking flow lacks a state parameter bound to the session
Linking request can be completed by any browser holding the code
No re-authentication before attaching a social identity
Linked identity change is not notified to the account owner

text: The OAuth provider validates redirect_uri with a string prefix rather than an exact match, so a registered callback path can be extended with traversal segments that land on another endpoint of the same application. An attacker crafts an authorization URL whose redirect target is a page that leaks the incoming query string, sends it to a victim with an active provider session, and captures the authorization code. The code is then exchanged at the legitimate callback for a session as the victim. The defect is imprecise redirect matching combined with a code that is not bound to the exact redirect target.

metadata.title: Authorization Code Theft via Lax redirect_uri Validation
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site
root_causes: redirect_uri validated by prefix or path prefix instead of exact match
Path traversal allowed inside the registered callback path
Authorization code not bound to the original redirect target
Code exchange possible from any client instance

text: The client application contains a redirect endpoint that forwards to any supplied path, and the OAuth provider accepts a redirect_uri that resolves through that endpoint. Because the implicit flow carries the access token in the URL fragment, the browser preserves it across the redirect and delivers it to the attacker's server. The attacker sends the crafted authorization URL to a victim with an active provider session and captures the token, then uses it to read the victim's API data. The defect is the combination of an open redirect and a token that travels in a redirectable URL.

metadata.title: Implicit-Flow Token Leakage Through an Open Redirect
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site
root_causes: Client application exposes an open redirect endpoint
Provider allows the callback path to be extended into that redirect
Access token carried in the URL fragment and forwarded by the redirect
No token binding to the original client page
associated_labs: OAuth Access Token Theft via Open Redirect

text: A client-side page forwards its own URL, including the OAuth token fragment, to its parent window through postMessage without checking the parent origin. Because the page can be framed by any site, an attacker embeds it, receives the message, and extracts the token. The OAuth callback itself may be framed or the proxy page may be reachable with the token in its fragment. The defect is an unrestricted cross-origin messaging channel that carries a credential, turning a minor client-side flaw into full token theft.

metadata.title: Token Exfiltration Through a postMessage Proxy Page
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
root_causes: Client page posts its full URL to any parent origin
No origin validation on postMessage sender or receiver
Token present in the framed page fragment
Attacker can frame the OAuth callback
associated_labs: OAuth Access Token Theft via a Proxy Page

text: The application parses the JWT to obtain the session subject but never verifies its signature, so any client can rewrite the payload and present it as valid. An attacker changes the sub claim from their own username to administrator, re-encodes the token, and keeps or blanks the original signature. Because the server only decodes, the modified claims are trusted. The defect is a verification gap in the session middleware, often introduced by using a decode helper that does not validate signatures by default.

metadata.title: JWT Claims Accepted Without Signature Verification
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature
root_causes: Server decodes the JWT payload but never verifies the signature
Session subject taken directly from the sub claim
Verification library called in decode-only mode
No test asserts that a tampered token is rejected

text: The server selects the verification algorithm from the token's own header and accepts the none algorithm, so a client can present an unsigned token and have it treated as valid. An attacker sets alg to none, removes the signature segment, and rewrites the claims. The server skips verification because the token declares that no signature is required. The defect is algorithm negotiation driven by attacker input instead of a pinned server-side choice.

metadata.title: Unsigned JWT Acceptance via alg=none
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature
root_causes: Server honours the alg header from the token
none algorithm permitted by the verification library
Signature segment allowed to be empty
Algorithm not pinned to a server-side allowlist

text: The service signs HS256 tokens with a short, guessable secret, so an attacker who captures one token can brute-force the key offline and then mint arbitrary tokens. Because HMAC verification is fast and the search space is a common password list, recovery takes seconds on commodity hardware. Once the secret is known, the attacker signs a token with an escalated subject and the server accepts it as genuine. The defect is key material with insufficient entropy, not the JWT format itself.

metadata.title: JWT Secret Recovery Through Offline Brute Force
root_causes: HMAC secret drawn from a small or common wordlist
Secret shared across environments and never rotated
No key strength requirement in provisioning
Symmetric signing used for multi-service identity

text: The verifier reads the jwk header from the token and uses that embedded public key to check the signature. Because the attacker supplies both the key and the signature, any token can be made self-consistent. The attacker generates an RSA key pair, embeds the public key in the header, and signs the modified claims with the private key. The server verifies successfully against the attacker's own key. The defect is circular trust: the credential carries its own verification material.

metadata.title: Self-Signed JWT via Injected jwk Header
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature
root_causes: Verifier trusts the jwk embedded in the token header
No check that the key belongs to a trusted source
Attacker-supplied key used to verify its own signature
Key identifier not bound to a server-side key store

text: The verifier supports the jku header and fetches the JSON Web Key Set from whatever URL the token specifies, without checking that the host is trusted. An attacker hosts a JWKS containing their own public key, points jku at it, and signs a modified token with the corresponding private key. The server retrieves the attacker's key set, finds a matching key, and accepts the forged token. The defect is an unvalidated outbound key fetch driven by attacker-controlled metadata.

metadata.title: Remote Key Set Substitution via jku Header
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature
root_causes: Verifier fetches JWKS from an unvalidated jku URL
No host allowlist for key set retrieval
Attacker-hosted key set accepted
No integrity check on retrieved keys

text: The verifier uses the kid header to locate a key file by concatenating it into a path, so a traversal sequence selects a different file with predictable contents. An attacker points kid at a known file such as /dev/null, which yields an empty key, and signs the modified token with that same empty key. The server loads the file, derives the key, and verifies the attacker's signature. The defect is unvalidated key identifier resolution through the filesystem.

metadata.title: Key File Selection via kid Path Traversal
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory
root_causes: kid concatenated into a filesystem path
No canonicalization or allowlist for key identifiers
Verifier accepts arbitrary files as key material
Errors leak the resolved key path

text: The verifier accepts both RSA and HMAC algorithms and chooses based on the token header, using the same key material for either. When the token declares HS256, the RSA public key is treated as the HMAC secret. Because the public key is published, an attacker can sign an arbitrary token with it. The server then verifies the HMAC using the public key bytes and accepts the forgery. The defect is missing binding between algorithm family and key type.

metadata.title: RSA Public Key Misuse as HMAC Secret
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature
root_causes: Verifier selects algorithm from the token header
RSA public key reused as an HMAC secret
No key-type binding between algorithm and key
Public key exposed at a predictable endpoint

text: The application does not publish its RSA public key, but it signs multiple JWTs with the same key pair. Given two signatures and the corresponding messages, an attacker can recover the RSA modulus and reconstruct the public key. With that key in hand, the attacker performs the same algorithm-confusion attack: declare HS256 and sign a forged token using the recovered public key bytes as the HMAC secret. The defect is both the recoverable key material and the missing algorithm-to-key binding.

metadata.title: Public Key Recovery From Signed JWTs
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature
root_causes: RSA public key not published but recoverable from signatures
Same RSA key pair used across tokens
Algorithm confusion still possible without a JWKS endpoint
No key-type binding in the verifier
associated_labs: JWT Algorithm Confusion Without an Exposed Key

text: The store applies a single-use discount by checking a usage counter and then incrementing it in separate steps. When many redemption requests arrive in the same narrow window, each reads the pre-increment value, concludes the coupon is still available, and applies the discount. The result is a limit overrun: one coupon is redeemed repeatedly and a high-value item is purchased far below its price. The defect is a non-atomic check-then-act sequence around a shared counter, not a flaw in the coupon rules themselves.

metadata.title: Coupon Limit Overrun Through Concurrent Redemption
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution Using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization
root_causes: Usage counter checked before it is incremented
Read-modify-write not atomic or serialized
Per-user limit enforced without a database constraint
No idempotency key on redemption requests

text: The login endpoint enforces a rate limit by incrementing a failure counter after each bad password, but concurrent requests all read the same pre-increment count. A burst of guesses therefore passes the limit check simultaneously, letting an attacker test far more passwords than the policy allows. Once the correct password is found, the attacker logs in and reaches the admin panel. The defect is a non-atomic counter around the authentication decision, which turns a rate limit into a suggestion.

metadata.title: Login Rate-Limit Bypass Through Concurrent Attempts
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
root_causes: Failed-attempt counter incremented after the credential check
Rate limit applied per request rather than per window
Counter update not atomic under concurrency
No account lock independent of request pacing
associated_labs: Rate Limit Bypass via Race Condition

text: The purchasing flow spreads cart mutations across several endpoints that do not share a consistent lock or version. By racing an add-item request against a cart-update or checkout request, an attacker causes the price validation to observe one state while the order commits another. A typical exploit adds an expensive item, then races a cheap gift-card credit against checkout so the total is computed from the discounted state while the expensive item ships. The defect is cross-endpoint state divergence.

metadata.title: Cross-Endpoint Race in Cart and Checkout
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution Using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization
root_causes: Cart state mutated by independent endpoints without a shared lock
Price captured at different times by validation and checkout
Gift-card credit applied before the cart total is fixed
No version check on the cart object

text: The change-email endpoint writes the requested address, generates a confirmation token, and sends the message in several steps without a per-account lock. Two concurrent requests with different addresses interleave so that the token generated for the attacker's address is validated against the privileged address, or the privileged address is stored while the attacker controls the confirmation. The attacker can then claim an address that carries administrator rights. The defect is a multi-step state transition exposed to concurrent execution.

metadata.title: Email Claim Race on a Single Endpoint
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution Using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization
root_causes: Confirmation token generated and bound in separate steps
Email field updated before verification completes
No per-account lock during change-email flow
Token not bound to the requested address

text: The password reset token is a hash of the username and the current timestamp rather than a random value, so anyone who knows the approximate generation time can enumerate the exact token. The attacker triggers a reset for the victim and, in the same instant, a reset for their own account. Because the attacker knows their own username and token, they recover the timestamp and compute the victim's token. The defect is predictable entropy: the token's only secret is a value the attacker can narrow to a small window.

metadata.title: Predictable Time-Based Password Reset Token
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-330: Use of Insufficiently Random Values
root_causes: Reset token derived from a timestamp and username
No cryptographic randomness in token generation
Token validity window wide enough to search
Token not bound to a server-side nonce

text: Registration creates the user record first and marks it verified later, leaving a window in which the account exists without a completed verification state. Concurrent registration requests with the same username but different addresses interleave so that the attacker can persist an arbitrary address before verification is enforced. The attacker then logs in with the unverified address and inherits any privileges attached to it. The defect is a partially constructed object exposed to concurrent readers and writers.

metadata.title: Registration Race Bypassing Email Verification
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution Using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization
root_causes: User object created before email verification completes
Verification flag absent rather than false during construction
No unique constraint or transaction around registration
Confirmation token bound to a mutable record

text: CWE-1284: Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input. The product accepts a numeric or semi-numeric value that denotes a quantity (size, length, frequency, price, rate, count, duration, or number of operations) without validating that the quantity has the required properties and lies within the domain's meaningful range. The flawed architectural assumption is that quantities arriving from a trusted UI or an authenticated client are inherently sane and that an upper-bound check alone is sufficient. Root causes include missing lower-bound and sign checks, implicit string-to-number coercion, unchecked multiplication of quantity by unit price, and trusting client-calculated totals. Signature-based WAFs and AST/SAST tools rarely flag it because the request is well formed and the endpoint is legitimate; exploitability emerges only from the semantic relationship between the quantity and downstream arithmetic, inventory, or resource allocation.

metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-1284: Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input

Implicit coercion of strings, arrays, or fractional values into integer quantities

text: CWE-1287: Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input. The product receives a value that is expected to be a specific type (string, integer, boolean, array, object, or a constrained format such as a digest or identifier) but validates only superficially or relies on implicit coercion. The flawed assumption is that the JSON parser, framework binder, or client SDK enforces the contract. Root causes include permissive deserialization, truthy coercion of strings such as "false", accepting arrays where a scalar is expected, and validating shape without validating format. SAST and WAF signatures miss it because the payload is syntactically valid JSON and the malicious effect appears only after the value crosses a language or service boundary where its type is reinterpreted.

text: CWE-1288: Improper Validation of Consistency within Input. The product receives a composite input whose fields must agree with one another (start before end, offset plus length within a buffer, debit equal to credit, quantity times unit price equal to total, declared length equal to actual payload) but validates each field in isolation. The flawed assumption is that the client constructs coherent objects and that per-field range checks imply cross-field correctness. Root causes include stateless field validation, duplicated calculations across services, and trusting a client-supplied total or hash. WAFs and SAST tools see only well-formed fields; the defect is the missing relational predicate between them, which manifests only when downstream logic consumes the inconsistent combination.

text: CWE-1289: Improper Validation of Unsafe Equivalence in Input. The product uses an input value as a resource identifier, hostname, path, extension, or redirect target, but compares it with an allowlist or trusted value without accounting for equivalent representations that downstream components treat differently. The flawed assumption is that string equality on the raw input equals semantic equality after canonicalization. Root causes include case-sensitive comparisons on case-insensitive systems, missing Unicode or punycode normalization, single-pass URL decoding, trailing-dot and dot-segment normalization differences, and extension checks that ignore case or alternate separators. WAF signatures miss it because the payload contains no forbidden literal; the bypass exists in the gap between the validator's parser and the consumer's parser.
