text: CWE-839: Numeric Range Comparison Without Minimum Check. The product validates that a numeric value is less than or equal to a maximum but omits the corresponding lower-bound check, so negative values pass. The flawed assumption is that the value is inherently non-negative because the UI slider, HTML input, or client SDK prevents negatives. Root causes include maximum-only validation, signed types used for quantities that should be unsigned, and comparisons that treat a negative as trivially satisfying 'less than max'. The defect is invisible to signature-based tooling because the payload is a valid number and the endpoint is legitimate; impact appears when the negative value reaches arithmetic, array indexing, memory operations, or balance updates.

text: CWE-190: Integer Overflow or Wraparound. The product performs arithmetic on a fixed-width integer and assumes the result remains representable, but the operation exceeds the type's range and wraps to a small or negative value. The flawed assumption is that quantities, lengths, counters, prices, or timestamps are bounded by business logic and therefore cannot reach the type limit. Root causes include unchecked multiplication of quantity by size or price, 32-bit counters for unbounded events, signed/unsigned conversions, and length arithmetic performed before allocation. SAST tools may flag some instances, but WAFs cannot detect the pattern because each request is individually valid; the overflow emerges from accumulated state or a single large but accepted value.

text: Business logic flaw: OTP verification is optional rather than mandatory during account signup. The backend creates the account and issues a session whenever the signup payload is otherwise valid, treating the absence of the `code` field as an acceptable state instead of a failed precondition. The flawed assumption is that the client always submits the verification step and that a missing field cannot occur outside the intended UI flow. Root causes include validating the OTP only when present, modeling verification as a client-side step rather than a server-side state transition, and issuing the session before ownership of the email is proven. The request is syntactically valid and uses the legitimate signup endpoint, so WAFs and SAST rules do not flag it; the defect is an absent server-side guard on a required workflow state.

root_causes: OTP comparison skipped when the verification field is absent or null

Verification modeled as a client step instead of server-side pending-registration state

text: Business logic flaw: cashback retailer entitlement is enforced in the mobile UI but not in the merchant-selection API. A non-premium account is limited to three selected retailers, yet the endpoint that updates the selection accepts an arbitrary merchant list, allowing the user to replace the initial three and accrue cashback across every retailer associated with the program. The flawed assumption is that the client's plan-aware UI is the authoritative enforcement point. Root causes include trusting client-supplied merchant identifiers and counts, missing a server-side plan-tier check on update, and treating the initial selection as immutable without enforcing that invariant in the data layer.

root_causes: Merchant list accepted from the client without a server-side plan-tier check
Selection count and merchant eligibility not enforced in the data layer
Plan limits enforced only by the mobile application UI

text: Business logic flaw: the organization's two-factor authentication requirement is enforced when a report is created but not when a collaborator is invited or accepts access. A reporter who has 2FA enabled can invite an account without 2FA, and the invitation is accepted without a step-up check, exposing the same sensitive report the policy was meant to protect. The flawed assumption is that the creator's 2FA status transitively covers every principal who later gains access. Root causes include checking authentication assurance at one workflow entry point, treating collaboration as a metadata operation, and failing to re-evaluate organization policy at access time.

metadata.report_title: Business Logic error leads to bypass 2FA requirement
root_causes: 2FA policy checked at report creation but not at collaboration acceptance
Invitation treated as metadata rather than a privilege grant on a protected object
No re-evaluation of authentication assurance on each access

text: Business logic flaw: product prices are fixed per currency and are not revalued against the current foreign-exchange rate at checkout. The client chooses the billing currency, and the server charges the static local price, so when the currency pair moves the customer can pay materially less than the USD list price. The flawed assumption is that published currency prices remain economically equivalent and that users will not select a currency for arbitrage. Root causes include treating currency as a display preference, storing independent price points without an FX source and timestamp, and failing to recompute the charge from a single base price at payment time.

metadata.title: Static Currency Pricing Enables Foreign-Exchange Arbitrage at Checkout
metadata.report_title: Business Logic, currency arbitrage - Possibility to pay less than the price in USD
root_causes: Independent static price points per currency with no FX source or timestamp
Client-selected currency treated as a display preference rather than a pricing input
Charge amount not recomputed from a single base price at payment time

text: Business logic flaw: the invitation endpoint accepts a client-supplied `access_level` and grants the corresponding role without verifying that the inviter's plan entitles them to assign it. The free plan is supposed to allow only edit access, while read-only access is a Pro feature; the UI hides the option, but the API trusts the request body. Root causes include enforcing plan entitlements only in the frontend, using the request value as the source of truth for role assignment, and failing to validate the role against the inviter's plan at invitation creation and acceptance.

text: Business logic flaw: the password-change flow accepts a new password without verifying the current password and without rejecting reuse of the existing password. Authorization is inferred solely from possession of a valid session, so any request that reaches the endpoint can rotate the credential. The flawed assumption is that an authenticated session proves the actor knows the current password and that users will choose a different value. Root causes include missing re-authentication, no comparison against the stored credential, and no post-change session invalidation. The request is a legitimate authenticated call, so signature-based controls do not flag it.

metadata.report_title: Business logic error
root_causes: Current password not required or verified before rotation

Other sessions and tokens not invalidated after a credential change

text: CWE-20: Improper Input Validation. The product accepts data whose type, range, format, or semantics it never verifies, then routes that data into a business decision such as pricing, entitlement, state change, or resource allocation. This is the parent class of most business-logic bypasses: the request is legitimate in shape, but the value falls outside the contract the downstream logic silently assumes. MITRE classifies this entry as Class with a mapping usage of DISCOURAGED, which means the entry is discouraged as a mapping target because it is too abstract to stand alone. The defect is rarely a single missing check; it is a mismatch between the contract each layer assumes and the data it actually receives. Root causes include validation performed only in the browser, mobile client, or API gateway, checks that confirm syntax but never confirm business meaning or allowed value sets, and validation applied to one representation while a second representation reaches the sink. Because the request is syntactically valid and targets a legitimate business endpoint, signature-based controls and generic SAST rules rarely flag the abuse. The effect becomes observable only when the attacker's action is compared with the intended business invariant and the persisted state.

text: CWE-1021: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers or Frames. The product allows another origin to frame it, so an attacker can overlay a trusted interface and trick a user into confirming a business action. Clickjacking turns authenticated user intent into an attacker-chosen transfer, approval, or permission grant. MITRE classifies this entry as Base with a mapping usage of ALLOWED, which means the entry is approved for direct mapping. The defect is rarely a single missing check; it is a mismatch between the contract each layer assumes and the data it actually receives. Root causes include missing or ineffective X-Frame-Options or Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors, frame protection removed for embedding by partners without origin restrictions, and sensitive actions not requiring re-authentication or confirmation. Because the request is syntactically valid and targets a legitimate business endpoint, signature-based controls and generic SAST rules rarely flag the abuse. The effect becomes observable only when the attacker's action is compared with the intended business invariant and the persisted state.

text: Business logic flaw: the order-placement workflow leaks the one-time password it is supposed to verify. When a wrong code is submitted, the validation error includes the expected session code, so the attacker reads the secret from the response and submits it successfully. The same workflow also trusts the phone number carried in the final order request rather than the number that was verified, allowing the attacker to place orders against arbitrary numbers. Root causes include echoing expected values in error messages, binding verification to a request field instead of a server-side session record, and treating the OTP step as a UI gate rather than a proof that must be carried forward.

metadata.title: Order OTP Bypass Through Session Code Disclosure in Validation Errors
metadata.report_title: Bypass OTP verification when placing Order
root_causes: Validation error echoes the expected OTP or session code to the client
Verified phone number not bound server-side to the order that follows
Final order request accepts a replacement phone number after verification

text: Business logic flaw: the per-item purchase limit is enforced only by disabling the plus control in the cart UI. The checkout URL carries item identifiers and quantities as cart:quantity pairs, and the backend accepts whatever quantities appear there, through the payment step. The attacker copies the checkout link, edits the quantities to values far above the published limit, and completes payment. Root causes include treating a UI affordance as the control, parsing quantities from a client-editable URL without re-checking the catalog limit, and performing no server-side validation between cart submission and payment.

metadata.title: Per-Item Purchase Limit Enforced Only in the Cart UI
metadata.report_title: [spectacles.com] Bypassing quantity limit in orders
root_causes: Quantity limit represented only by an inactive plus button in the client
Checkout URL accepts arbitrary item:quantity pairs without catalog validation
No server-side limit check at cart submission or payment initiation

text: Business logic flaw: order quantities are accepted as fractional numbers and multiplied into the total, so a quantity of 0.1 for a dish priced at 99 reduces the charge to 9.9 while the kitchen still prepares a full portion. The behavior is consistent across the cart-calculation and order-placement requests, so the tampered total survives to the payment gateway. Root causes include a numeric quantity field without an integer constraint, a total computed from the client-supplied quantity rather than from a validated line item, and no minimum-charge or quantity check at order placement.

metadata.title: Fractional Food Quantity Reducing the Order Total Below the Dish Price
metadata.report_title: [www.zomato.com] Tampering with Order Quantity and paying less amount then actual amount, leads to business loss
root_causes: Quantity accepted as a decimal without an integrality constraint
Order total derived from client-supplied quantity and unit cost
No minimum charge or fulfilment check when the quantity is below one

text: Business logic flaw: the ticket add-on seat count is submitted as a multipart field such as addon-268-number-of-seats-0 with a value like 3-seats-3, and the server trusts both the count and the derived price from that field. Changing the value to 10-seats-10 adds ten seats while the order total remains zero, allowing unlimited free bookings. Root causes include a composite client-controlled field encoding both quantity and price, no server-side lookup of the add-on price, and no validation that the submitted total matches the catalog price for the selected quantity.

metadata.title: Ticket Seat Count Tampering Zeroing the Order Total
metadata.report_title: attacker can book unlimited tickets in free at https://aaf.com/checkout/order-received/21237/?key=wc_order_5bbef48fa35b2
root_causes: Composite seat field encodes quantity and price from the client
Add-on price not resolved from the catalog server-side
Order total accepted without comparing to the recomputed amount

text: Business logic flaw: the endpoint that sends an OTP to a subscriber also returns the OTP to the caller in the network response, so the verification step proves nothing. The attacker enters any subscriber number, reads otpKey from the response, submits it to the prompt, and gains the ability to change that subscriber's plan. Root causes include generating the OTP client-side or including it in the API payload for convenience, no binding between the OTP and the subscriber session, and treating the possession of a request as proof of control over the phone number.

metadata.report_title: OTP bypass - Unintended disclosure of OTP to client allows attacker to manage users' subscriptions
root_causes: OTP included in the send-otp API response body
No separation between the issuance channel and the verification channel
Subscriber number accepted without proof of control

text: Business logic flaw: the subscription state machine grants paid entitlements even when no payment has settled. The attacker selects a paid plan with a card that cannot be charged, receives a payment-failure notification, increases the seat count, receives another failure, then cancels the subscription. After cancellation the account continues to use paid features despite never having paid. Root causes include treating cancellation as a state that preserves entitlements, a payment-failure path that leaves the plan active, and no reconciliation between invoice settlement and feature gating.

metadata.title: Paid Features Retained After a Failed Payment and Subscription Cancellation
metadata.report_title: [app.lemlist.com] Improper handling of payment lead to bypass payment
root_causes: Entitlement granted before payment settlement is confirmed
Cancellation preserving paid features instead of reversing the plan
Payment-failure branch leaving the subscription active

text: Business logic flaw: accepting a promotional fee discount is not idempotent and does not mark the offer as consumed, so every call to the acceptance endpoint applies the full discount again. A twenty-thousand dollar offer replayed thirty times produced six hundred thousand dollars of fee-free processing. Root causes include an acceptance handler that creates a credit entry per request, no unique constraint or consumed flag on the offer, and no reconciliation between the offer value and the total credit applied.

metadata.title: Fee Discount Acceptance Endpoint Replayable Without Idempotency
metadata.report_title: Fee discounts can be redeemed many times, resulting in unlimited fee-free transactions
root_causes: Offer acceptance not idempotent and not marked consumed
Credit entry created per request without a uniqueness constraint
No cap comparing total applied credit with the offer value

text: Business logic flaw: coupon validation checks only that the code exists and is active, then recalculates shipping to zero without recording a redemption. The same free-shipping code can therefore be applied to every order indefinitely, and a code disclosed in a public report remains usable by anyone. Root causes include no per-account or global usage counter, no redemption log, no expiration enforcement, and a validation path that never consults prior use.

metadata.report_title: Unlimited Reuse of Coupon Code Allows Free Shipping on All Orders on a Merch Store
root_causes: Coupon validity checked without a usage count or redemption record
No per-account or global redemption cap
Disclosed promotional code left active indefinitely

text: Business logic flaw: the ad review and payment gate is represented by mutable fields on the ad object, and the advertiser-facing API accepts writes to admin_approval and effective_status. A PATCH request setting admin_approval to APPROVED, configured_status to ACTIVE, and effective_status to ACTIVE makes the campaign live without review or payment details, and the platform even sends an approval confirmation. Root causes include exposing internal review fields in the public update schema, trusting client-supplied status, and having no server-side transition that validates the required preconditions.

metadata.title: Ad Approval and Effective Status Writable Through the Campaign API
metadata.report_title: Able to approve admin approval and change effective status without adding payment details.
root_causes: Internal review and status fields accepted by the public update endpoint
No server-side state machine enforcing review and prepayment preconditions
Approval confirmation driven by the client-supplied status value

text: Business logic flaw: partner invitations no longer require the recipient to prove control of the invited email address. An attacker can create an account using a victim employee's email, accept the pending owner invitation, and obtain owner privileges in the partner account. A low-privilege member can also harvest the invited owner's address from the member list and use the same gap to escalate. Root causes include removing the invitation link verification step, allowing account creation without email verification, and binding invitation acceptance to the email string rather than to a verified identity.

metadata.report_title: Shopify Partners Invitation Process Allows Privilege Escalation Without Email Verification
root_causes: Invitation acceptance no longer verifies the email link or token

Invitation bound to an email string rather than a verified identity

text: Business logic flaw: the workspace user limit counts only active members when invitations are issued, so an administrator can pre-invite any number of users before reaching the limit. Each invited user can then join simply by signing up and verifying their email, even after the workspace is at its plan cap. Root causes include a limit check that ignores pending invitations, no re-check at acceptance time, and a plan model that counts only realized memberships.

metadata.report_title: User Limit Bypass via Pending Invitations in Workspace System

No limit re-check when a pending invitation is accepted
Pending invitations not reserved against the plan quota

text: Business logic flaw: the requirement to enable two-factor authentication before inviting team members is enforced in the client. The application blocks the invite action based on a flag returned to the browser, and the server processes the invitation request without re-checking the account's 2FA state. Changing the flag from false to true with an intercepting proxy or match-and-replace rule lets the user send invitations with 2FA disabled. Root causes include a security decision made in the presentation layer, no server-side prerequisite check on the invitation endpoint, and trusting a boolean supplied by the client.

metadata.report_title: 2FA requirement bypass when inviting team members
root_causes: 2FA prerequisite evaluated only in the client response
Invitation endpoint does not re-check the account's 2FA state
Client-supplied boolean trusted as proof of a security condition

text: Business logic flaw: the approval workflow intends to prevent approval of a file whose contents changed after review, using the file ETag as a freshness token. The backend enforces the comparison only when the etag field is present and non-empty. Removing the field from the approval JSON body lets the approver approve or reject a file whose content was modified after review. Root causes include treating the freshness parameter as optional, no server-side retrieval of the current version for comparison, and a fail-open default when the client omits the binding value.

metadata.title: Approval Freshness Check Skipped When the ETag Parameter Is Omitted
metadata.report_title: Approval app's file-freshness check can be bypassed by omitting the etag parameter, allowing approval of unreviewed file changes
root_causes: ETag comparison skipped when the parameter is absent or empty
Current file version not loaded server-side for the decision
Missing binding treated as acceptable instead of rejected

text: Business logic flaw: the CampTix Instamojo add-on never binds an Instamojo payment to the CampTix order. Three paths share the root cause: the return handler marks a draft order pending using only the ticket payment token, the notification handler fails open when the MAC is invalid, and the MAC-valid Credit path applies COMPLETED using a ticket token taken from the query string that the MAC does not cover. A legitimate cheap payment can therefore complete a different, more expensive order. Root causes include a fail-open authentication branch, security-relevant data outside the signed payload, and no stored payment request identifier or amount for comparison.

metadata.title: Payment Webhook Fails Open and Credits Orders Without Binding the Payment
metadata.report_title: Instamojo CampTix: fail-open MAC + webhook Credit without binding payment to order
root_causes: Invalid MAC still marks the ticket pending instead of rejecting
Ticket token taken from the unsigned query string while the MAC covers only the body
Payment request identifier and amount never stored and compared with the order

text: Business logic flaw: the second-factor gate is coupled to the presence of a refresh cookie rather than to a server-side verified state. After a correct password the application issues session cookies including bb_refresh and shows the OTP page. Deleting bb_refresh and refreshing the page lands the user in the authenticated application without ever submitting the OTP. Root causes include issuing a fully privileged session before the second factor completes, treating a missing cookie as an already verified state, and having no server-side flag that distinguishes password-only sessions from fully authenticated ones.

metadata.title: Deleting the bb_refresh Cookie Bypasses Email OTP Two-Factor Authentication
metadata.report_title: Email OTP/2FA Bypass
root_causes: Full session issued before the second factor is verified
Missing refresh cookie treated as verified instead of unauthenticated
No server-side distinction between password-only and fully authenticated sessions

text: Business logic flaw: the commission fee is calculated as bounty_award / 100 * 20 and then rounded to two decimal places, so an award of one or two cents produces a fee of 0.002 or 0.004 that rounds to 0.00. Splitting a reward into many micro-payments therefore pays the recipient the full amount while evading the twenty percent platform fee. Root causes include rounding each fee independently instead of accumulating the exact amount, allowing awards below the minimum fee unit, and having no reconciliation between total awards and total fees.

metadata.title: Commission Fee Rounded to Zero on Micro-Bounty Awards
metadata.report_title: Rounding errors on rewarding a bounty leads to bypassing the 20% H1 commission fee
root_causes: Fee rounded per transaction to the currency's display scale
Minimum award below the smallest fee unit accepted
No reconciliation between total awarded and total fee collected
